title: Ethiopian Roasted Barley Powder
community: All of Ethiopia — the ancient energy food of travellers and farmers
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Besso — dry roasted barley grain ground to a coarse powder, mixed with a little water or honey into a paste or eaten dry. The ancient Ethiopian travel food and field snack — carried by farmers, soldiers, pilgrims, and traders for centuries. No cooking required on the journey.
longDesc: Besso is one of Ethiopia's most ancient foods — essentially raw food technology, roasted and ground so it requires no cooking to eat. It is the predecessor of modern protein powders and energy bars, carried in small pouches and mixed with water or honey on demand. Nutritious, lightweight, long-lasting, and completely self-sufficient.
ingredients: // To eat: water or honey to mix, and salt
equipment: Grain mill, blender, or mortar and pestle
steps: Heat a heavy dry pan over medium heat.
Add barley grain. Toast, stirring constantly, for 15—18 minutes until deeply golden and fragrant.
Grind to a coarse powder in a grain mill or blender.
To eat: mix 2—3 tbsp besso with enough water or honey to form a thick paste.
chefTips: Toast more deeply than you think — under-toasted besso tastes raw and starchy.
The grinding should be coarse — besso has texture.
On a journey: carry besso dry. Add water from any clean source.
commonMistakes: Fine grinding — besso should be coarse.
cookingScience: See ETH018 for the science of roasted grain. Besso's pre-roasting converts the raw starch to partially gelatinised starch — making it more digestible without cooking and giving it a shelf life of months without preservation.
sustainabilityTips: Besso is the ultimate sustainable food — no packaging, no refrigeration, made from one ingredient.
servedWith: On its own as a snack
storage: Dry in an airtight container — indefinitely.
culturalNote: Besso is the food that Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrims carried on their long journeys to Lalibela, that farmers carried to the fields at dawn, that soldiers carried on campaigns across the highlands. It has sustained Ethiopian people for millennia without refrigeration, without cooking, and without anything except a handful of water.
